claims.evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The SET1 locus in the Chr5 region is hypothesised to be caused by the ABA‐HYPERSENSITIVE GERMINATION 1 (AHG1) gene.
claims.source: The SET1 locus in this region is hypothesised to be caused by the ABA‐HYPERSENSITIVE GERMINATION 1 (AHG1) gene (Footitt et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claims.claim: AHG1 is a type 2C protein phosphatase (PP2C) that inhibits ABA signalling via dephosphorylating class II SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2), which promote seed dormancy by activating ABA-responsive transcriptional changes.
claims.source: AHG1 is a type 2C protein phosphatase (PP2C) that inhibits ABA signalling via dephosphorylating class II SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2), which promote seed dormancy by activating ABA-responsive transcriptional changes (Liu and Hou, 2018; Née et al., 2017a; Nishimura et al., 2007, Nishimura et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claims.claim: DOG1 has been shown to directly bind to AHG1, independently from ABA, and inhibit its function, thus allowing DOG1 to inhibit germination via the ABA pathway.
claims.source: DOG1 has been shown to directly bind to AHG1, independently from ABA, and inhibit its function, thus allowing DOG1 to inhibit germination via the ABA pathway (Carrillo-Barral et al., 2020; Née et al., 2017a; Nishimura et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claims.claim: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: Mutants of all three candidate genes have altered ABA sensitivity: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2007), while dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity (Née et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claims.claim: dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: Mutants of all three candidate genes have altered ABA sensitivity: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2007), while dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity (Née et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The dog1-3 mutant in the Col-0 background consistently had reduced CV of germination time, and reduced mean and mode days to germination compared to the wild type.
claims.source: We tested these mutants for their effects on germination time distributions and found that the dog1-3 mutant in the Col-0 background (Bentsink et al., 2006) consistently had reduced CV of germination time, and reduced mean and mode days to germination compared to the wild type (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: The dog1 mutant in the No-0 background showed a similar phenotype to dog1-3 in Col-0, with reduced CV, mean and mode.
claims.source: The dog1 mutant in the No-0 background showed a similar phenotype to dog1-3 in Col-0, with reduced CV, mean and mode (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C.

claims.claim: Reduced ABA sensitivity of the dog1 mutants in the Col-0 and No-0 backgrounds was observed in germination assays, with higher levels of exogenous ABA required to observe a change in the germination fraction.
claims.source: Consistent with previously published work (Née et al., 2017a), we observed reduced ABA sensitivity of the dog1 mutants in the Col-0 and No-0 backgrounds in our germination assays, with higher levels of exogenous ABA required to observe a change in the germination fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, D).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, D and comparison to published work.

claims.claim: The ahg1-5 mutant in the Col-0 background showed a slight increase in CV of germination time, which was associated with an increase in ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: On the other hand, the ahg1-5 mutant in the Col-0 background (Née et al., 2017a) showed a slight increase in CV of germination time, which was associated with an increase in ABA sensitivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E, F).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E, F.

claims.claim: Both DOG1 and AHG1 candidate genes for the Chr5 locus have an effect on the CV of germination time which is consistent with their altered ABA sensitivities.
claims.source: Thus, both of these candidate genes for the Chr5 locus have an effect on the CV of germination time which is consistent with their altered ABA sensitivities.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claims.claim: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background, a slight increase in CV was observed, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH.
claims.source: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background (Li et al., 2014), we observed a slight increase in CV, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 3 DAH), but did not see a convincing phenotype in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing (i.e. in the same conditions as the MAGIC lines used for QTL mapping) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 30 DAH).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G.

claims.claim: A convincing phenotype for the anac060 mutant was not seen in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing.
claims.source: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background (Li et al., 2014), we observed a slight increase in CV, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 3 DAH), but did not see a convincing phenotype in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing (i.e. in the same conditions as the MAGIC lines used for QTL mapping) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 30 DAH).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G.

claims.claim: A weak tendency towards an increase in ABA sensitivity in the anac060 mutant was observed, but this was not as striking as that reported in seedlings.
claims.source: We observed a weak tendency towards an increase in ABA sensitivity in the anac060 mutant, but this was not as striking as that reported in seedlings (Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison to published work.

claims.claim: The candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity and suggest that this could also be the case for the ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claims.claim: The ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity and suggest that this could also be the case for the ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claims.claim: A simplified mathematical model of the core ABA-GA network that governs germination time was built.
claims.source: To answer this, we built a simplified mathematical model of the core ABA-GA network that governs germination time (Liu and Hou, 2018; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claims.claim: The model includes both ABA and GA since the decision to germinate is governed by the relative levels of the two hormones.
claims.source: We reasoned that it was necessary to include both ABA and GA in the model since the decision to germinate is governed by the relative levels of the two hormones (Née et al., 2017b; Shu et al., 2016b), and both converge to regulate the expression of a common set of transcription factors that control seed dormancy and germination (Liu and Hou, 2018; Piskurewicz et al., 2008; Shu et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: This is a justification for the model structure based on cited literature.

claims.claim: The model represents the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator.
claims.source: We represent the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator, which we assume must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: The model assumes that Integrator must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
claims.source: We represent the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator, which we assume must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: The model assumes that ABA promotes the production of Integrator and that GA promotes its degradation.
claims.source: We assume that ABA promotes the production of Integrator and that GA promotes its degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: The model assumes that Integrator promotes ABA production and inhibits GA production.
claims.source: Integrator is assumed to promote ABA production and inhibit GA production.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: The model includes a factor, Z, that increases upon sowing and promotes GA production.
claims.source: A factor, Z, increases upon sowing and promotes GA production.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: Modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions observed experimentally.
claims.source: A simple stochastic model of the ABA-GA network shows that modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally.
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results.

claims.claim: Varying the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production can cause correlated effects on CV and mode.
claims.source: To investigate the effect of ABA sensitivity on germination time distributions in the model, we varied the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production, which is inversely correlated with the sensitivity to ABA (see Materials and methods). Varying this parameter can cause correlated effects on CV and mode (Figure 5B) and can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable (i.e. more peaked), to more variable (i.e. long tailed) (Figure 5C), that qualitatively match the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally (Figure 1A, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Varying the ABA threshold for Integrator production parameter can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable to more variable, that qualitatively match the range observed experimentally.
claims.source: To investigate the effect of ABA sensitivity on germination time distributions in the model, we varied the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production, which is inversely correlated with the sensitivity to ABA (see Materials and methods). Varying this parameter can cause correlated effects on CV and mode (Figure 5B) and can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable (i.e. more peaked), to more variable (i.e. long tailed) (Figure 5C), that qualitatively match the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally (Figure 1A, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: As the sensitivity of integrator to ABA increases, the germination time distributions are more long tailed with a higher CV and mode.
claims.source: As the sensitivity of integrator to ABA increases (lower values of ABA threshold for integrator production), the germination time distributions are more long tailed with a higher CV and mode (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: With low sensitivity to ABA, the model is monostable after sowing, with the high GA, low ABA, low Integrator (germination) steady state the only stable state after the sowing-induced rise in GA production.
claims.source: With low sensitivity to ABA, the model is monostable after sowing, with the high GA, low ABA, low Integrator (germination) steady state the only stable state after the sowing-induced rise in GA production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: With higher ABA sensitivity, the model is bistable after sowing and the rise in GA production, with a low GA, high ABA, high integrator (non-germination) steady state in addition to the germination steady state both existing after sowing.
claims.source: With higher ABA sensitivity, the model is bistable after sowing and the rise in GA production, with a low GA, high ABA, high integrator (non-germination) steady state in addition to the germination steady state both existing after sowing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, I).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the bistable scenario, after the rise in GA production, seeds can remain in the non-germination steady state for some time but are driven to transition to the germination steady state by stochastic fluctuations, which results in variable germination times and a later average germination time.
claims.source: In this bistable scenario, after the rise in GA production, seeds can remain in the non-germination steady state for some time but are driven to transition to the germination steady state by stochastic fluctuations, which results in variable germination times and a later average germination time (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The bistable regime is associated with an increase in CV and mode of germination time.
claims.source: Hence, the bistable regime is associated with an increase in CV and mode of germination time (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The coupled variation in CV and mode of MAGIC line germination time distributions can be at least partly accounted for by variation in the parameter controlling the sensitivity of integrator production to ABA.
claims.source: Thus, the coupled variation in CV and mode of MAGIC line germination time distributions can be at least partly accounted for by variation in the parameter controlling the sensitivity of integrator production to ABA: as the sensitivity to ABA increases, the model becomes bistable, with later and more variable germination times.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claims.claim: Once within the bistable regime, increases in ABA sensitivity increase the stability of the non-germination steady state.
claims.source: Additionally, once within the bistable regime, increases in ABA sensitivity increase the stability of the non-germination steady state (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O–U compared with Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–N).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Increases in the stability of the non-germination steady state can result in an increasing proportion of seeds remaining in this state and not germinating (decreasing percentage germination) and can also further increase the variability of germination time of the seeds that do germinate.
claims.source: This can result in an increasing proportion of seeds remaining in this state and not germinating (decreasing percentage germination) and can also further increase the variability of germination time of the seeds that do germinate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q–U compared to Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines.
claims.source: Hence, we hypothesise that natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause (i) the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines and (ii) differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claims.claim: Natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
claims.source: Hence, we hypothesise that natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause (i) the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines and (ii) differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claims.claim: The model can capture multiple possible relationships between the CV and mode of germination time distributions, with the nature of the relationship changing depending on which parameter was being varied.
claims.source: We found that the model could capture multiple possible relationships between the CV and mode of germination time distributions, with the nature of the relationship changing depending on which parameter was being varied.
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results from parameter screens.

claims.claim: A number of parameters showed positively correlated effects on CV and mode.
claims.source: A number of parameters showed positively correlated effects on CV and mode (e.g. Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), although the strength of this correlation varied depending on the region of parameter space and the parameter being changed (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Positive correlations between effects on CV and mode were observed for parameters controlling the rates of basal production and degradation of GA, ABA and Integrator as well as for those controlling the GA-dependent degradation rate of the Integrator.
claims.source: Positive correlations between the effects on CV and mode were also observed for the sensitivity of ABA production to Integrator levels (we define sensitivity as the inverse of the Integrator threshold for promotion of ABA production and use the equivalent definition for all subsequent sensitivity parameters; see Figure 5—figure supplement 4E).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Multiple other parameters in addition to that governing ABA sensitivity could account for the positive correlation between CV and mode of germination time distributions in the MAGIC lines.
claims.source: Thus, multiple other parameters in addition to that governing ABA sensitivity (Figure 5B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4F, G) could account for the positive correlation between CV and mode of germination time distributions in the MAGIC lines.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claims.claim: In most cases, low percentage germination tends to be associated with high CV and mode while high percentage germination tends to be associated with low CV and mode.
claims.source: In most cases, low percentage germination tends to be associated with high CV and mode while high percentage germination tends to be associated with low CV and mode, similar to the correlations observed within the MAGIC lines (e.g. see Figure 5B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results and comparison to experimental data.

claims.claim: Some parameters showed both correlated and anti-correlated effects on CV and mode and some generated decoupled changes in CV and mode.
claims.source: For example, for the parameter controlling basal GA production and that controlling the rate of Integrator production, in addition to the positively correlated effects on CV and mode described above, anti-correlated effects on these traits were also observed in other regions in parameter space (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B, C).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: For some areas of parameter space, anti-correlated effects on CV and mode occurred when modulating the sensitivity of the Integrator to GA-promoted degradation.
claims.source: For some areas of parameter space, anti-correlated effects on CV and mode occurred when modulating the sensitivity of the Integrator to GA-promoted degradation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4F, H).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, 3, and 4.

claims.claim: Somewhat decoupled changes in CV and mode were observed when varying the parameter that controls the level of noise in the system, such that, for some regions of parameter space, reductions in noise decreased the CV while maintaining a relatively constant mode and percentage germination.
claims.source: Somewhat decoupled changes in CV and mode were also observed when varying the parameter that controls the level of noise in the system, such that, for some regions of parameter space, reductions in noise decreased the CV while maintaining a relatively constant mode and percentage germination (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D, Figure 5—figure supplement 4G, H).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, 3, and 4.

claims.claim: Across a range of parameter sets, both modes and CVs of germination times tend to be higher when bistability rather than monostability occurs after the sowing-induced rise in GA production.
claims.source: We found that across a range of parameter sets, both modes and CVs of germination times tend to be higher when bistability rather than monostability occurs after the sowing-induced rise in GA production (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The model predicts that high variability in germination time is associated with the ABA-GA network operating in the bistable regime.
claims.source: Thus, in general, the model predicts that high variability in germination time is associated with the ABA-GA network operating in the bistable regime.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claims.claim: The model predicts that starting from germination time distributions with low or high variability, increasing concentrations of exogenous ABA will initially increase the CVs of the germination time distributions.
claims.source: The model predicts that starting from germination time distributions with low or high variability, increasing concentrations of exogenous ABA will initially increase the CVs of the germination time distributions (Figure 6Ai), causing long-tailed distributions to emerge (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The addition of exogenous ABA stabilises the high Integrator, high ABA, low GA non-germination state, requiring stronger fluctuations to allow germination.
claims.source: This is because the addition of exogenous ABA stabilises the high Integrator, high ABA, low GA non-germination state, requiring stronger fluctuations to allow germination (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: At higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, the germination time distribution becomes flattened into a seemingly uniform distribution with a high mean and therefore lower CV.
claims.source: At higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, the germination time distribution becomes flattened into a seemingly uniform distribution with a high mean and therefore lower CV (Figure 6Ai, ii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, [ABA]exo = 2.5).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The increase of exogenous ABA also reduces the percentage of germinated seeds.
claims.source: Hence, the increase of exogenous ABA also reduces the percentage of germinated seeds (Figure 6Aiv).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6Aiv.

claims.claim: ABA treatments tended to increase the spread of germination time distributions, particularly for low variability lines.
claims.source: ABA treatments tended to increase the spread of germination time distributions, particularly for low variability lines.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claims.claim: In the low variability lines, high ABA concentrations of 5 and 10 μM caused large increases in the CV of germination time, such that the distributions of germination times for low variability lines treated with ABA were similar to those of high variability lines in control conditions.
claims.source: In the low variability lines, high ABA concentrations of 5 and 10 μM caused large increases in the CV of germination time, such that the distributions of germination times for low variability lines treated with ABA were similar to those of high variability lines in control conditions (Figure 6Bi, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, compare Col-0, 5 and 10 μM [ABA]exo with M182, 0 μM [ABA]exo).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The experimental observation that the moderate ABA dose of 5 μM caused larger increases in CV compared with the changes in the mode was consistent with the model.
claims.source: The experimental observation that the moderate ABA dose of 5 μM caused larger increases in CV compared with the changes in the mode was also consistent with the model (Figure 6Ai, iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, [ABA]exo = 0 compared to [ABA]exo = 1.5).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claims.claim: For high variability lines, increasing concentrations of ABA increased mean and mode germination times, but had relatively little effect on CV.
claims.source: For high variability lines, increasing concentrations of ABA increased mean and mode germination times, but had relatively little effect on CV (Figure 6Bi-iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, M182).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Consistent with a less striking effect of exogenous ABA on the CV of high variability lines compared to low variability lines, in the model, the fold changes in CV upon ABA addition for high variability lines were smaller than those predicted for low variability lines.
claims.source: Consistent with a less striking effect of exogenous ABA on the CV of high variability lines compared to low variability lines, in the model, the fold changes in CV upon ABA addition for high variability lines were smaller than those predicted for low variability lines (Figure 6Ai).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claims.claim: Addition of exogenous GA to high and low variability lines in the simulations led to a reduced mode and less variable germination times.
claims.source: In contrast to ABA treatments, addition of exogenous GA to high and low variability lines in the simulations led to a reduced mode and less variable germination times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1Ai, iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Addition of GA can destabilise and even destroy the high Integrator, high ABA and low GA non-germination steady state.
claims.source: This is because addition of GA can destabilise and even destroy the high Integrator, high ABA and low GA non-germination steady state (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B), causing the model to become monostable.
claims.evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: When added experimentally to high and low variability MAGIC lines, GA tended to decrease the level of variability in germination time, with the effect strongest for the high variability genotypes.
claims.source: As predicted by the model, when added experimentally to high and low variability MAGIC lines, GA tended to decrease the level of variability in germination time, with the effect strongest for the high variability genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, M182).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to model predictions.

claims.claim: High GA addition increased germination percentages and tended to decrease the mean germination time in high variability lines.
claims.source: As expected from previous studies (Bewley, 1997; Koornneef and Karssen, 1994; Ni and Bradford, 1993), high GA addition also increased germination percentages and tended to decrease the mean germination time in high variability lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to previous studies.

claims.claim: For low variability lines, GA had little effect on the variability (CV), percentage germination, mean or mode germination times.
claims.source: For low variability lines, GA had little effect on the variability (CV), percentage germination, mean or mode germination times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, Col-0) as these lines germinated in a less variable manner with high percentage germination even in the absence of GA.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For both ABA and GA, the overall effects of exogenous addition were qualitatively similar between the model and experiments.
claims.source: Thus, for both ABA and GA, the overall effects of exogenous addition were qualitatively similar between the model and experiments.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claims.claim: Loss of function of the CYP707A1 enzyme caused the Col-0 germination time distribution to become more long-tailed, with a small shift in the mode days to germination of ~1 day.
claims.source: Similar to the effect of exogenous addition of ABA on low variability lines, loss of function of the CYP707A1 enzyme caused the Col-0 germination time distribution to become more long-tailed, with a small shift in the mode days to germination of ~1 day (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Loss of both CYP707A1 and CYP707A2 enzymes severely inhibited germination time and caused a large increase in the mode days to germination, similar to the effect of higher concentrations of exogenous ABA.
claims.source: Loss of both enzymes severely inhibited germination time and caused a large increase in the mode days to germination, similar to the effect of higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, which in both cases is related to the germination time distribution becoming more uniform (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The correlated effect found on CV, mode and percentage germination due to a change in the ABA degradation rate is consistent with the results from changing the ABA degradation parameter in the model.
claims.source: The correlated effect we found on CV, mode and percentage germination due to a change in the ABA degradation rate is also consistent with the results from changing the ABA degradation parameter in the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 4Ai-iii).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claims.claim: The ga3ox1-3 ga3ox2-1 mutant, which has reduced GA levels, showed an increased CV and, similar to the cyp707a1-1 cyp707a2-1 mutant, had increased mode and decreased percentage germination.
claims.source: To test genetically the effect of decreasing the GA concentration on the germination time distribution of Col-0, we used the ga3ox1-3 ga3ox2-1 mutant, which lacks two enzymes involved in GA biosynthesis (Mitchum et al., 2006). This double mutant, which has reduced GA levels (Mitchum et al., 2006), showed an increased CV and, similar to the cyp707a1-1 cyp707a2-1 mutant, had increased mode and decreased percentage germination (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7 and comparison to cited literature.

claims.claim: The findings on GA and ABA dose–response experiments and mutants support the model predictions regarding the effects of altering ABA and GA levels on CV, mode and percentage germination.
claims.source: Together with the GA and ABA dose–response experiments, these findings support the model predictions regarding the effects of altering ABA and GA levels on CV, mode and percentage germination.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claims.claim: Variability in seed germination time is relevant for plant survival in the wild, where high variability may function as a bet-hedging strategy.
claims.source: Variability in seed germination time is relevant for plant survival in the wild, where high variability may function as a bet-hedging strategy.
claims.evidence: This is based on theoretical considerations and cited literature.

claims.claim: The advantages of variability in the wild contrast to the situation in agriculture, where minimal levels of variability are desirable to promote crop uniformity needed for optimal harvests.
claims.source: The advantages of variability in the wild contrast to the situation in agriculture, where minimal levels of variability are desirable to promote crop uniformity needed for optimal harvests (Finch-Savage and Bassel, 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to literature on agriculture.

claims.claim: Germination time distributions are genetically controlled since they can vary greatly between different lines and are reproducible for a given genotype.
claims.source: By describing detailed distributions of germination time for hundreds of Arabidopsis lines grown in a common environment, our work reveals that these distributions are genetically controlled since they can vary greatly between different lines and are reproducible for a given genotype.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Candidate genes underlying the loci identified may alter germination time through influencing ABA sensitivity.
claims.source: Using this natural variation, we identified two loci underlying variability and present evidence that candidate genes underlying the loci may alter germination time through influencing ABA sensitivity.

results.result: Extensive natural variation in seed germination time variability exists among Arabidopsis accessions and MAGIC lines, with CVs ranging from 0.09 to 1.7. This variation is reproducible across independent experiments and storage conditions, with broad-sense heritability estimated at ~40%.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C28-C33 provide converging experimental evidence from multiple independent experiments showing reproducible variation in germination time variability across hundreds of lines. The heritability estimate (C33) is appropriately compared to published values, and reproducibility is demonstrated across different seed harvests (C31) and storage periods (C32).

results.result: Variability in germination time arises independently of positional or developmental gradients within plants or siliques. Seeds from individual siliques show the full range of germination times observed in whole-plant samples, with no consistent differences between top and bottom halves of siliques.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by experimental data showing that variability exists within single siliques and is not dependent on position along the silique. The experimental design appropriately controls for positional effects, though the mechanism generating this variability remains unidentified.

results.result: Within the MAGIC population, germination time variability (CV) shows weak correlations with modal germination time and percentage germination, but these traits can be uncoupled.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by statistical analysis and visualization of the data (Figure 3). The weak correlations are quantified, and specific examples demonstrate that lines can have similar modes but different CVs, supporting the conclusion that these traits can be partially decoupled.

results.result: QTL mapping identified two genetic loci contributing to germination time variability: one on Chr3 (~16 Mb, accounting for ~14% of variance) and one on Chr5 (~18.6-19.8 Mb, accounting for ~9% of variance). The Chr3 QTL affects multiple germination traits, while the Chr5 QTL specifically affects variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C42-C55 are supported by QTL mapping in MAGIC lines and independent validation through bulk-segregant analysis in F2 populations. The statistical significance is appropriately assessed with genome-wide thresholds. The Chr5 QTL is independently validated (C52-C54), strengthening the conclusion. Together, the two QTL account for only 23% of variance (C134), indicating additional loci likely exist.

results.result: Candidate genes at the identified QTL (ANAC060 at Chr3, DOG1 and AHG1 at Chr5) are implicated in modulating ABA sensitivity. Mutant analysis shows that dog1 mutants have reduced CV and reduced ABA sensitivity, while ahg1 mutants show increased CV and increased ABA sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C56-C68, C72-C73 are based on literature citations for candidate gene functions (C57-C63) and experimental testing of mutants (C64-C68). While dog1 and ahg1 mutants show effects consistent with altered ABA sensitivity (C64-C68), the anac060 mutant shows inconsistent phenotypes depending on storage conditions (C69-C71), weakening support for ANAC060 as the causal gene. The connection between candidate genes and QTL effects remains correlative rather than definitively causal, as the natural allelic variants have not been directly tested.

results.result: A stochastic mathematical model of the ABA-GA network shows that modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions observed experimentally. Varying the ABA threshold for Integrator production causes correlated effects on CV and mode, producing distributions from less variable to more variable that qualitatively match experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C74-C84 describe the model structure and its ability to reproduce experimental observations. The model is appropriately justified based on known biology (C75), and simulations demonstrate that varying ABA sensitivity generates distributions matching experimental data (C82-C84). However, the model is simplified and represents multiple proteins as a single 'Integrator' variable, which limits mechanistic insight.

results.result: The model operates in monostable or bistable regimes depending on ABA sensitivity. In the bistable regime, seeds can remain in a non-germination state until stochastic fluctuations drive transition to germination, resulting in higher CV and mode. High variability in germination time is associated with the ABA-GA network operating in the bistable regime.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93, C102-C103 describe the model's dynamical behavior and its relationship to germination variability. The bistable switch mechanism is well-characterized through nullcline analysis and simulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The hypothesis that natural variation arises from differences in ABA sensitivity affecting bistability (C92-C93) is a reasonable inference from the modeling results, though it remains speculative without direct experimental validation.

results.result: Parameter screens reveal that multiple model parameters beyond ABA sensitivity can affect the relationship between CV and mode. Some parameters show positively correlated effects, others show anti-correlated or decoupled effects, capturing the complex relationships observed in MAGIC lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C101 are supported by extensive parameter screens (Figure 5—figure supplements 2-4). The analysis demonstrates that the model can capture diverse relationships between germination traits depending on which parameters vary, consistent with the weak correlations observed experimentally. This suggests that undetected genetic variation in multiple network components may contribute to the observed phenotypic variation (C135).

results.result: Model predictions on exogenous ABA addition were validated experimentally. ABA treatment increases CV in low variability lines, making their distributions similar to high variability lines in control conditions. For high variability lines, ABA increases mode but has little effect on CV. The overall effects of exogenous ABA were qualitatively similar between model and experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C104-C112, C118 demonstrate good qualitative agreement between model predictions and experimental observations for ABA dose-response experiments. The model correctly predicts that ABA will increase CV in low variability lines (C109-C110) and have less effect on CV in high variability lines (C111-C112). However, the agreement is qualitative rather than quantitative, and some high variability lines show slight decreases in CV with ABA (C111), which is not fully explained.

results.result: Model predictions on exogenous GA addition were validated experimentally. GA treatment decreases CV and mode in high variability lines by destabilizing the non-germination steady state. For low variability lines, GA has little effect as these lines already germinate with low variability and high percentage germination.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 show good qualitative agreement between model predictions and experimental observations for GA dose-response experiments. The model correctly predicts that GA will decrease variability in high variability lines (C115) and have minimal effect on low variability lines (C117). The mechanistic explanation through destabilization of the non-germination state (C114) is supported by nullcline analysis.

results.result: Genetic perturbations of ABA and GA levels validate model predictions. Loss of ABA catabolism enzymes (cyp707a1, cyp707a1 cyp707a2) increases CV and mode, while loss of GA biosynthesis enzymes (ga3ox1-3 ga3ox2-1) increases CV and mode. These effects are consistent with model predictions for altered ABA and GA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 provide genetic validation of the model through mutant analysis. The effects of cyp707a mutants (increased ABA) and ga3ox mutants (decreased GA) on germination distributions are consistent with model predictions and with the hormone dose-response experiments. This convergent evidence from multiple approaches strengthens support for the model.

results.result: Germination time distributions are genetically controlled and can vary greatly between lines. Candidate genes underlying identified loci may alter germination time through influencing ABA sensitivity. Modeling and experiments show that perturbation of the ABA-GA network can modulate variability in germination times in a predictable manner, suggesting that high or low variability could be specifically selected for in the wild and in crop breeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 summarize the main findings of the study. The genetic control of germination distributions is well-supported by the reproducibility data and QTL mapping (C126). The role of ABA sensitivity is supported by candidate gene analysis and mutant studies, though not definitively proven (C127). The predictable modulation of variability through the ABA-GA network is supported by the validated model (C128). The suggestion about selection (C129) is a reasonable inference but remains speculative without direct evidence.

results.result: Variability in germination time exists even for seeds from the same silique, suggesting it can arise independently from developmental gradients in the plant. Seeds from proximal and distal halves of siliques have similar germination behaviors, indicating variability is likely not caused by gradients of regulatory molecules along the fruit.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 are supported by experimental data showing variability within single siliques and no consistent differences between silique halves (Figure 2). This rules out simple positional or developmental gradient explanations for the observed variability.

results.result: The Chr3 and Chr5 QTL together account for only 23% of the variance in CV in the MAGIC lines. Undetected genetic variation in multiple components of the ABA-GA network may contribute to the variation in germination time distributions and the complex relationship between CV, mode, and percentage germination.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 acknowledge the limitations of the QTL mapping. The low percentage of variance explained (C134) is clearly stated and indicates that additional loci exist. The suggestion that undetected variation in multiple network components contributes to the observed phenotypic variation (C135) is a reasonable inference supported by the parameter screen results showing that multiple parameters can affect germination traits.

results.result: The model behaves as a time-dependent toggle switch with stochastic fluctuations, which can be used as a framework to understand variable germination behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 describe the model's behavior and its utility as a conceptual framework. The time-dependent toggle switch behavior is well-characterized through the modeling analysis, and the framework successfully accounts for the observed variability in germination times.

results.result: The level of variability in germination times is an important trait that does not always correlate with percentage germination. Future work should characterize the effects of germination regulators on CV as well as on percentage germination and average germination time.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 emphasize the importance of measuring variability as a distinct trait from percentage germination. This is well-supported by the data showing weak correlations between these traits (C39-C41). The recommendation for future work (C145) is a reasonable suggestion based on the findings.

results.result: Germination time is a plausible system for studying the genetics of inter-individual variability.
results.evaluation: Claim C148 is supported by the demonstration that germination time variability is a robust, heritable trait that varies between natural accessions. The successful QTL mapping and model validation establish germination time as a tractable system for studying phenotypic variability.

results.result: Phenotypic variability among genetically identical individuals can promote species survival in unpredictable environments through bet-hedging strategies. In plants, theoretical and ecological studies support that variability in germination time is advantageous in unpredictable environments. This contrasts with agriculture, where minimal variability is desirable for crop uniformity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C17, C124-C125 provide context from the literature on bet-hedging and phenotypic variability. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies. The contrast between wild and agricultural contexts (C125) is well-established in the literature.

results.result: The decision to germinate is controlled by the balance between ABA (which represses germination) and GA (which promotes germination). These hormones function in a mutually antagonistic manner, and the ABA-GA network can act as a bistable switch with two possible states: dormant (high ABA, low GA) or germinating (low ABA, high GA).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C18-C27 summarize established knowledge about seed dormancy and the ABA-GA network. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to the literature and provide necessary background for the study. The bistable switch behavior has been previously demonstrated experimentally and through modeling (C25-C27).

results.result: Previous studies showed that in some Arabidopsis accessions, seeds matured on primary inflorescences had different germination behaviors than those on branches, and developmental differences along the inflorescence could create differences in seed germination time between fruits.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 cite previous work on positional effects in Arabidopsis. These claims provide context for the current study's investigation of within-silique variability and are appropriately supported by citations.

results.result: Previous work suggests that feedback on ABA biosynthesis and catabolism can modulate variability in ABA concentrations, and that genes involved in ABA response show high variability in expression between seedlings. The decision to germinate is likely made by groups of cells in the embryonic root, though it is unclear how noise in individual cells influences this multicellular decision.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C143 cite relevant literature on ABA regulation, gene expression variability, and the multicellular nature of germination decisions. These claims provide context for discussing the model's limitations and potential mechanisms of variability generation. The citations are appropriate and the discussion acknowledges uncertainties (C139).

results.result: Multiple aspects of Arabidopsis development display phenotypic variability. A common feature across studies is that multiple QTL affect variability of a trait, with some also affecting the average trait value and others not.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C147 cite literature on phenotypic variability in other Arabidopsis traits and compare the findings to the current study. The comparison is appropriate and helps contextualize the results within the broader field of variability genetics.
